title: Naaman (2 Kings 5)
hookLine: a proud general is told to wash seven times in a muddy river

lines: A GREAT GENERAL, AND A LEPER.
cards: The person who sets this story moving doesn't even get a name. She's a little girl from Israel, carried off by raiders from Syria, now a servant to the wife of the Syrian army's commander.
That commander is Naaman: a great man, honored, brave, rich, and a leper. And one day this captive girl says to her mistress: I wish my master were with the prophet in Samaria. He would heal him.
One sentence of kindness from a kidnapped child, and a general packs up silver, gold, ten changes of clothes, and a letter from his king.

teach.b: Naaman arrives at Elisha's door with his horses and chariots, the full parade. And Elisha doesn't even come out.
He sends a messenger with a short instruction, in the Douay-Rheims: "Go, and wash seven times in the Jordan." Naaman is furious.

He'd pictured the prophet coming out, calling on his God, waving a hand over the spot, something worthy of a general. And the Jordan? Aren't the rivers of Damascus better than all the waters of Israel?
He turns to leave in a rage.

teach.h: IF HE'D ASKED A GREAT THING.
teach.b: Then his servants gently say: "if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing, surely thou shouldst have done it: how much rather what he now hath said to thee: Wash, and thou shalt be clean?"
He asked for something simple. So Naaman goes down to the river and dips himself seven times.
And his flesh, the Douay says, became "like the flesh of a little child." Like the girl who started all this. He goes back and says: now I know there is no God in all the earth but in Israel.
Elisha refuses any payment at all.

teach.h: WASH, AND THOU SHALT BE CLEAN.
teach.b: Notice who carried the healing to Naaman: a captive girl, a messenger, his own servants.
Jesus remembers him in the synagogue at Nazareth: many lepers in Israel in Elisha's time, and none was cleansed but Naaman the Syrian.
Catholic tradition sees baptism here: going down into the water, coming up like a newborn. The Church reads this story in Lent, as people prepare for baptism at Easter.

how: Catholics hear Naaman's healing at Mass in Lent, alongside Jesus recalling him at Nazareth, and the Church has long read his washing in the Jordan as a figure of baptism.

games.q: you're Naaman. you've come all this way, and the prophet won't even come to the door. he says wash seven times in the Jordan. what do you do?
o: go home and wash in the rivers of Damascus.
demand that the prophet come out.
listen to your servants, and go down to the Jordan.
games.why: after storming off, he listens to his servants, washes seven times, and his flesh becomes like a little child's.

practice: Think of a problem where the answer is probably small, the apology you could just say, the doctor you could just call, the early night, and you've been waiting for something bigger.
If a voice says that's too simple to matter, that's Naaman at the riverbank; if you pray, ask for the humility to go down to the water.

wordCard.voice: Naaman. The proud Syrian general healed of leprosy when he finally did the simple thing and washed seven times in the Jordan. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the skin disease translated leprosy, a broader term than the disease called leprosy today.

carryVoice: Your line: go and wash. And that's week fifty-nine: wisdom, the Temple, the widow's jar, Carmel, the whisper, the mantle, and Naaman. Day four hundred thirteen, in the books.
